chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Currencies Move - The Building Blocks

lessons.title: What Determines an Exchange Rate: Demand, Supply and the RBI's Managed Float

body.text: An exchange rate is not a value handed down by a government. It is a price, set the same way any traded price is set: by how much of a currency people want to buy against how much they want to sell, at that moment.

children.text: Open any business news app and you will see a line like "USD/INR: 87.42" scroll past, usually with a red or green arrow next to it. Most investors treat that number the way they treat a cricket score: something happening in the background, occasionally alarming, rarely explained. That is a mistake if you hold or plan to hold anything priced outside India: a US mutual fund, an offshore real estate deal, gold, or even an Indian company whose earnings depend heavily on exports or imported inputs. This course builds, from the ground up, the machinery that actually moves that number. This first lesson starts with the most basic question: what makes one rupee worth more or less against one dollar, and why does the Reserve Bank of India let it move at all instead of just fixing it?
The Exchange Rate as a Price, Not a Fixed Number

markDefs.definition: The exchange rate for immediate delivery of a currency, settled within two business days. Contrast this with a forward rate, which is agreed today for delivery on a future date and is used to hedge currency risk in advance.

children.text: The rate you see quoted, USD/INR 87.42, is the

: how many rupees one US dollar fetches right now in the interbank market. Every second, thousands of buyers and sellers of dollars and rupees, banks acting for exporters, importers, foreign investors, and each other, are placing orders. When dollar buyers outnumber dollar sellers, the dollar gets more expensive in rupee terms, and the rupee is said to depreciate. When sellers outnumber buyers, the dollar gets cheaper and the rupee appreciates. Nobody at the RBI sits down each morning and decides the number. The number is an outcome of that order flow, the same way a stock's price on the NSE is an outcome of buy and sell orders hitting the exchange, not a value assigned by SEBI.

body.text: None of these flows individually sets the rupee's level. The spot rate at any instant is simply the price at which the sum of all this buying and selling clears. This is exactly why a single headline, such as "oil prices rose" or "FPIs sold Indian bonds," is never a complete explanation for a currency move on its own. You have to net it against everything else happening that day.

children.text: Three Currency Regimes, and Where India Actually Sits

Not every country lets demand and supply decide its exchange rate freely. Broadly, there are three regimes, and India's is often described loosely and inaccurately as one of the extremes. Getting this right matters, because it changes what you should expect the RBI to actually do when the rupee moves sharply.

body.caption: Fixed peg vs free float vs managed float

cells: Fixed / hard peg
Central bank commits to a specific rate and defends it by buying or selling unlimited amounts of foreign currency
Hong Kong dollar, pegged to the US dollar in a tight band since 1983
Free float
Central bank does not intervene; the market rate is whatever demand and supply produce, with no target level
US dollar against most major currencies; the Fed does not manage the dollar's level
Managed float
Market sets the rate day to day, but the central bank intervenes occasionally to smooth sharp or disorderly moves, without defending a fixed level
The Indian rupee, managed by the RBI

children.text: The RBI has said this in almost the same words across multiple monetary policy statements over the years: it does not target any particular level for the rupee, and it intervenes only to curb excessive volatility, not to fight the underlying trend. This distinction matters enormously in practice. When the rupee weakened past 80 to the dollar for the first time in July 2022, the RBI sold dollars from its reserves, but it never tried to push the rate back below 80. It slowed the pace of the fall, absorbed some of the shock, and let the rupee find a new range. The same pattern showed up again as the rupee moved past 85 and then 87 through 2024 and 2025: intervention to reduce the speed of the move, not a fight to defend a specific number.

children.text: Where You Can Actually Watch This Happen

This is not something you need a Bloomberg terminal to observe. The NSE runs a currency derivatives segment, regulated by SEBI, where USDINR, EURINR, GBPINR and JPYINR futures trade in real time, alongside the equity segment most retail investors already know for Nifty and Sensex-linked products. If you have a Zerodha account, the currency segment on Kite shows you the same USDINR futures moving tick by tick during market hours, driven by exactly the demand and supply forces in the table above. Watching that price move for a week, next to RBI or news headlines about FPI flows or crude oil prices, is one of the fastest ways to build real intuition for this subject, faster than any textbook explanation.

body.title: Before You Read Any "Rupee Falls to Record Low" Headline
steps: Check whether other emerging market currencies (Indonesian rupiah, South African rand, Brazilian real) moved the same way that day. A broad dollar rally is a different story from a rupee-specific problem
Check whether the move coincided with a large one-day FPI outflow from NSE or BSE listed equities and bonds
Check crude oil prices; India imports roughly 85% of its crude, so a spike is a common and mechanical driver
Check whether the RBI issued any statement or intervened, visible indirectly through a sudden change in reserves data
Only after checking these, decide whether this is a broad dollar story, an India-specific story, or a mix of both

body.title: Diagnose a Rupee Move
body.scenario: On a single trading day, the rupee depreciates by 0.8% against the dollar, its sharpest one-day fall in several months. That same day, Brent crude oil rises 4%, FPIs sell a net ₹3,200 crore of Indian equities, and the US Dollar Index (DXY) also rises against a broad basket of currencies, not just the rupee.
body.prompt: A colleague says "the rupee is collapsing, something is badly wrong with the Indian economy." Is that colleague's framing correct? What would you say instead, using only the facts given?
body.modelAnswer: The framing is too narrow. Three separate forces are visible here, and at least two of them are not India-specific: a broad dollar rally (shown by the DXY rising against many currencies, not just the rupee) and higher crude oil prices, which mechanically raise dollar demand from Indian importers regardless of the domestic economy's health. The FPI outflow is the one India-specific piece, and even that could simply be profit booking or a global risk-off move that also hit other emerging markets. Nothing here points to a structural problem with the Indian economy; it points to a day where several global and mechanical pressures aligned in the same direction. The correct response is to check whether other emerging market currencies moved similarly before concluding anything is uniquely wrong with India.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Which statement best describes the RBI's actual approach to managing the rupee, based on this lesson?
options: The RBI fixes the rupee at a specific rate against the dollar and defends that level, similar to Hong Kong's peg
The RBI never intervenes in the currency market under any circumstances, letting the rupee float completely freely like the US dollar
The RBI lets the market set the rupee's level day to day, and intervenes occasionally to smooth excessive volatility, not to defend a fixed target
The RBI sets the rupee's value once a year during the Union Budget and holds it there
body.explanation: This is the definition of a managed float, and it is explicitly how the RBI has described its own approach in monetary policy communications. The rupee crossing 80, then 85, then 87 against the dollar over recent years, each time with intervention that slowed but did not reverse the move, is the practical evidence of this in action.

children.text: Why This Matters Before You Look at Rates or Trade Data

markDefs.definition: A currency depreciating means it buys less of another currency than before, for example the rupee needing more rupees to buy one dollar. Appreciating means the opposite: it buys more.

children.text: The rest of this course builds specific forces on top of this demand and supply foundation: interest rate differentials in Chapter 2, the trade and current account deficit in Chapter 3, and capital flows and RBI intervention mechanics in more depth in Chapter 4. Every one of those forces works by shifting demand or supply for rupees and dollars, exactly as in the table above; they simply give you sharper, more specific reasons for why one side of that table grew heavier on a given day or over a given year. If you are holding offshore assets, gold, or an alternative investment with dollar-linked returns, a currency
in the rupee can add to your INR-denominated returns even if the underlying asset's dollar price barely moves. Chapter 5 comes back to exactly this, once you have the full toolkit.

cards.definition: The exchange rate for immediate delivery of a currency, settled within two business days.
A regime where the market sets the exchange rate day to day, but the central bank intervenes occasionally to smooth volatility without defending a fixed level. This is India's regime.
A currency becoming worth more relative to another currency; it buys more of the other currency than before.
A currency becoming worth less relative to another currency; it buys less of the other currency than before.
Foreign currency and gold assets held by the RBI, used partly to intervene in the currency market and cushion the economy against external shocks.

body.text: Figures cited in this lesson, including forex reserves, FX turnover, import cover and historical USD/INR levels, are approximate and rounded for teaching purposes. They change frequently and should be verified against current RBI and NSE data before being used in any real investment decision. Nothing in this lesson is investment advice.

points: An exchange rate is a market-clearing price, set by the balance of demand and supply for two currencies, not a number fixed by a government
Exporters, importers, FPI flows, remittances and RBI intervention are the main day-to-day sources of USD/INR demand and supply
There are three broad currency regimes: fixed peg, free float, and managed float. India runs a managed float, meaning the RBI smooths volatility but does not defend a specific level
A single headline driver, like an FPI outflow or an oil price spike, is rarely the whole story; check whether the move is broad-based across other emerging market currencies too
NSE's SEBI-regulated currency derivatives segment, accessible through brokers like Zerodha, lets you watch USDINR move in real time and build practical intuition
The rest of this course adds specific mechanisms, interest rates, trade balances, and capital flows, on top of this same demand and supply foundation
